cards.text: On 5 Nov the US sanctioned a Kuala Lumpur company in Prince Group's scam network. Malaysian reports we found named the Malaysian man sanctioned that day. None named the company.
cards.sub: The man is Chui Kok Wa, who OFAC says led a scam network in Madagascar. The company is Greenmeadows Properties Sdn Bhd.
sources: US Treasury press release sb0683, 5 Nov 2026: 4 individuals and 41 entities under E.O. 13581; Greenmeadows 'Malaysia-based'; Chui 'led an extensive network of scammers located in Madagascar' [brief S1]
OFAC Recent Actions 5 Nov 2026, SDN entries GREENMEADOWS PROPERTIES SDN BHD (Kuala Lumpur address) and CHUI, Kok Wa ('nationality Malaysia') [S2]; Federal Register 91 FR 72626-72627 [S3]

Malaysian coverage opened 18 Nov 2026: The Star 6 and 7 Nov, The Sun, The Vibes, RTM, Oriental Daily: all six name Chui as Malaysian, none names Greenmeadows or any Malaysian company [S16a-f]; search log in brief VERIFICATION GAPS 5

cards.h: Greenmeadows Properties Sdn Bhd, a KL holding company set up in December 2018, is the only Malaysian company among the 41 Prince Group entities the US added on 5 Nov.
cards.s: Treasury says its director is Dai An, a Prince Group leader it sanctioned in June. It names nothing the company itself did. The 181 targets of the two earlier rounds carry no Malaysian address.
cards.d: OFAC's 5 Nov 2026 action designated 41 entities under E.O. 13581 as part of the Prince Group transnational criminal organisation: 23 Cambodian, 8 BVI, 6 Hong Kong, 2 Singapore, 1 Mauritius and 1 Malaysian (count from the SDN entries). The Malaysian entry is Greenmeadows Properties Sdn Bhd, Kuala Lumpur, 'Organization Established Date 03 Dec 2018', 'Activities of holding companies', registration 201801044010, 'Linked To: DAI, An'. Treasury's release says Dai An, designated on 23 Jun 2026 as 'a high-level leader in the Prince Group TCO', 'serves as director for ... Malaysia-based Greenmeadows Properties Sdn Bhd'. The Federal Register designates the company under s.1(a)(ii)(C) of E.O. 13581: owned or controlled by, or having acted for or on behalf of, Dai An. The release alleges no specific conduct by Greenmeadows itself; its sentences about concealing assets and evading sanctions describe the action as a whole. Neither earlier Prince Group round (146 targets, 14 Oct 2025; 35 targets, 23 Jun 2026) shows a Malaysian address on OFAC's listing pages. Ownership of Greenmeadows is not established: the SSM record was not obtained. A designation is an administrative determination; OFAC runs a delisting process.
sources: US Treasury press release sb0683, 5 Nov 2026, Dai An and Greenmeadows paragraph [S1]
OFAC Recent Actions 5 Nov 2026 SDN entries (jurisdiction count) [S2]; Federal Register 91 FR 72627, E.O. 13581 s.1(a)(ii)(C) [S3]
Treasury sb0538, 23 Jun 2026 and OFAC Recent Actions 23 Jun 2026 (Dai An) [S4a, S4b]; Treasury sb0278 and OFAC Recent Actions 14 Oct 2025 (146 targets) [S5a, S5b]

cards.h: Singapore does not enforce US sanctions either. Its police used the US and UK releases to advance a laundering case and have seized or barred the sale of over S$500m in assets.
cards.s: Singapore Police had financial intelligence on Prince Group's chairman from 2024 and arrested three Singaporeans. No Malaysian agency has made a public statement on any of the three US rounds.
cards.d: Singapore Customs: 'Singapore does not enforce unilateral sanctions imposed by other countries.' Singapore Police said that, with 'the additional information obtained from the US's and UK's press releases on 14 Oct 2025', they advanced an investigation begun in 2024 on Suspicious Transaction Reporting Office intelligence on Chen Zhi and associates, and on 30 Oct 2025 seized or issued prohibition of disposal orders over more than S$150 million in assets. On 3 Mar 2026 they reported three Singaporeans arrested between November 2025 and January 2026 and assets 'seized and/or prohibited' worth 'more than S$500 million'. For Malaysia, no statement from PDRM, the Home Ministry, Bank Negara, SSM, Wisma Putra or the AGC on Greenmeadows, Chui Kok Wa or any of the three Prince Group rounds (Oct 2025, Jun 2026, Nov 2026) was found as at 18 Nov 2026. That is a finding about public statements only: suspicious transaction reports and investigations are confidential under AMLA ss.14 and 35. Caveat for the comparison: Singapore's case targeted assets and people in Singapore; no source shows Prince Group assets in Malaysia.
sources: Singapore Police Force, 31 Oct 2025 and 3 Mar 2026 releases [S13a, S13b]
Singapore Customs, 'Sanctioned Lists and Red Flags' and UNSC sanctions overview pages [S14a, S14b]
Search log for a Malaysian response, brief VERIFICATION GAPS; AMLA ss.14, 35 (AGC text as at 1 Mar 2026, pp.32, 61-62) [S8]

cards.h: Bank Negara's rules make a bank file a suspicious transaction report on any match with another country's sanctions list. A freeze is required only for UN and Malaysia's terrorism lists.
cards.s: Under AMLA s.44, an agency may freeze property once a Malaysian investigation into an unlawful activity has begun, including a certified foreign serious offence. A US listing alone does not trigger it.
cards.d: BNM policy document BNM/RH/PD 030-14 (effective 6 Feb 2024), para 27.8.3, marked 'S' (a requirement whose breach 'may result in enforcement action'): 'Reporting institutions shall submit a suspicious transaction report if there is any positive name match with individuals or entities listed in other unilateral sanctions lists.' The same rule recurs at 28.7.3 and 29.7.3. Para 27.3.11 (guidance): institutions 'may monitor and consolidate other countries' unilateral sanctions lists'. Freezing duties (27.6) attach only to the Domestic List (Home Minister's AMLA s.66B orders, terrorism only) and the UNSCR List (s.66C). AMLA s.44(1): an enforcement agency 'may issue an order to freeze any property of any person' where 'an investigation with regard to an unlawful activity has commenced against that person' and it has reasonable grounds to suspect proceeds; 'unlawful activity' includes a 'foreign serious offence' stated in a certificate issued by the foreign State. Ministers have said Malaysia recognises only UN Security Council sanctions (PM Anwar, 7 Nov 2023; Home Minister Saifuddin Nasution, 9 May 2024). Unclear: whether 27.8.3 binds institutions that do not load unilateral lists, since 27.3.11 is optional.
sources: BNM policy document BNM/RH/PD 030-14, legend p.15; paras 27.3.11 p.114, 27.6 p.115, 27.8.3 p.117 [S9]
AMLA (Act 613), AGC updated text as at 1 Mar 2026: s.3 pp.10-11, 14; s.44 pp.66-67; ss.66B-66C pp.99-103 [S8]
FMT 9 May 2024 (Home Minister); The Star 7 Nov 2023 (PM) [S15a, S15b]

cards.text: Washington's list obliges Malaysia to freeze nothing. Bank Negara's own rulebook still obliges every bank that finds a match on it to report one.
sources: BNM policy document paras 27.6 and 27.8.3 [S9]; AMLA s.66B-66C [S8]; ministers' UN-only statements [S15]

cards.text: It is like a foreign police notice naming a house on your street. You need not arrest anyone on it, but a neighbourhood that never knocks has made a choice too.
sources: Rests on the reframe's sources: no freeze duty on unilateral lists, STR duty on a match [S9]; AMLA s.44 needs a Malaysian investigation [S8]

cards.text: Any investigation of a KL company on Prince Group's US list can stay confidential. Whether anyone in Malaysia has looked at it need not. No agency has said.
sources: Confidentiality: AMLA ss.14, 35 [S8]; no public statement found as at 18 Nov 2026 (brief search log)

headline_suggestion: Prince Group sanctions reach a KL company; the Malaysian reports we found didn't name it
context_suggestion: On 5 Nov 2026 the US Treasury sanctioned 45 more targets in Cambodia-based Prince Group's network and, separately, a Malaysian it says led scams from Madagascar. Malaysia recognises only UN sanctions.
sources: US Treasury sb0683 (5 Nov 2026), sb0538 (23 Jun 2026), sb0278 (14 Oct 2025); OFAC Recent Actions 5 Nov 2026, 23 Jun 2026, 14 Oct 2025 (SDN entries); Federal Register 91 FR 72624-72630; USAO-DC press release 27 Oct 2026; affidavit in support of criminal complaint, US v. Chui Kok Wa et al. (D.D.C., sworn 23 Oct 2026); AMLA (Act 613) AGC text as at 1 Mar 2026; BNM policy document BNM/RH/PD 030-14 (2024); Singapore Police Force releases 31 Oct 2025 and 3 Mar 2026; Singapore Customs sanctions pages; FMT 9 May 2024; The Star 7 Nov 2023; Malaysian coverage of 5 Nov action (The Star, The Sun, The Vibes, RTM, Oriental Daily)
confidence: Medium-High. HIGH on the US record (Treasury release, OFAC SDN entries, Federal Register, DOJ release, sworn affidavit) and on Malaysian legal texts (AMLA AGC text as at 1 Mar 2026; BNM policy document). MEDIUM on the coverage claim: six Malaysian items opened, wider searches found none naming the company, but absence cannot be proven, so the hook says 'reports we found'. LOW on whether any Malaysian agency has acted: STRs and investigations are confidential by law, so the cards claim only that no public statement was found.
needs_verification: Re-run the Malaysian coverage search at publication (English, Malay, Chinese press, Bernama): the hook's 'None named the company' rests on six items opened plus searches as at 18 Nov 2026.
Re-check for any public statement from PDRM, the Home Ministry, BNM, SSM, Wisma Putra or the AGC on Greenmeadows or Chui Kok Wa at publication; fact 2's sub and the view depend on there being none.
SSM record for Greenmeadows Properties Sdn Bhd (not obtained; paid search): status, directors, shareholders. Cards say only what OFAC and Treasury state; never 'Dai An's company' or 'owned by'.
BNM para 27.8.3 scope: whether the STR duty binds institutions that do not load unilateral lists (27.3.11 is optional). The reframe says 'every bank that finds a match', which holds either way.
Singapore figures: 'seized and/or prohibited' > S$500 million (SPF, 3 Mar 2026). Card uses 'seized or barred the sale of'; confirm the gloss matches 'prohibition of disposal orders'.

Fact 1 sub: '181 targets of the two earlier rounds carry no Malaysian address' = 146 (14 Oct 2025) + 35 (23 Jun 2026) per Treasury counts, from text search of OFAC listing pages; some names recur under aliases.
source_notes: (1) Chui Kok Wa: Treasury says he defrauded Americans 'of over $400,000 equivalent'; the DOJ complaint alleges 'at least approximately $516,695' from about 74 wallets. Different agencies and bases; neither figure is on the cards. The US instrument is a criminal complaint (D.D.C.), not an indictment, despite The Record's headline. Chui is designated under E.O. 13694 (cyber), not as part of Prince Group. (2) Malaysian coverage: all six items opened name Chui as Malaysian; the working thesis that Malaysian coverage missed the Malaysian end was wrong and is narrowed to the company. (3) Which UN body: the 2022 foreign minister named the General Assembly; the PM (2023) and Home Minister (2024) named the Security Council; statute (AMLA s.66C) and BNM rules track the Security Council, so cards say UN. (4) All allegations originate with the US government (single-origin); attribution is kept on every card. (5) Kosmo's 31 Oct headline says Chui was arrested; no source supports an arrest; not used.
guardrails_applied: Designation framed as a US administrative act; no card says the company laundered, hid or held anything; 'names nothing the company itself did' stated on fact 1.
Chui named only with OFAC attribution ('who OFAC says led'); no loss figures, no 'indicted', no 'arrested', no birth date, ID or street address.
No 'Malaysia cannot freeze' and no 'Malaysia did nothing': fact 3 states the freeze route (AMLA s.44) and fact 2 says 'no public statement', with the confidentiality caveat in the detail.
Hook says 'reports we found', not 'Malaysian media ignored'.
Singapore comparison carries its caveat in the detail: its case targeted assets in Singapore; no source shows Prince Group assets in Malaysia.
View avoids issue 2017's 'stay out of Washington's sanctions and still...' shape; reframe uses an obligation contrast, not 'X is not Y'.
No ethnic descriptor for any person; DOJ's 'tied to China' language not used.
